title: Quantum state tomography through multi-frequency Josephson effect
authors: Xian-Peng Zhang, Ting-Rui Hu, Zhen-Biao Yang, Rubén Seoane Souto, Yugui Yao
abstract: Macroscopic quantum effects emerge when the coherent behavior of countless microscopic quantum states manifests collectively at a visible scale, as exemplified by the supercurrent carried by innumerable finite-momentum Cooper pairs. By rigorously analyzing the time evolution of superconducting nanodevices including finite-momentum superconductors and quantum-dot Josephson junctions, we analytically derive the ubiquitous macroscopic supercurrent that originates from quantum interference between distinct many-body eigenstates, which we term as the dynamic interference supercurrent. The dynamic interference supercurrent in a system of two Andreev spin qubits exhibits multi-frequency Josephson effect in the absence of external voltage and is governed by the response of the many-body eigenfunctions ($\vert r\rangle$) to variations in the superconducting phase $φ$, determined by the $φ$-space Berry connection $C_{rr'}=\langle r|\partial_φ|r'\rangle$. The macroscopic dynamic interference supercurrent, an inherent property of the superposition state itself, enables an advanced quantum entanglement measurement of the Andreev spin qubits. These findings open new avenues for investigating superconducting nanodevice properties from a wave-function level, with substantial implications for advancing quantum science and technology in solid-state superconducting devices, such as quantum computer, communication, memory, and sensor.
summary: This theoretical paper develops a method to measure quantum entanglement in superconducting qubits by analyzing the dynamic interference supercurrent (DIS). The DIS arises from quantum interference between different many-body eigenstates and is shown to be sensitive to the relative phases of the quantum state. This technique offers a pathway to perform quantum state tomography using only electrical measurements on superconducting nanodevices.
main_problem: To derive and utilize the dynamic interference supercurrent (DIS) as a novel, electrical method for performing quantum state tomography and measuring entanglement in superconducting qubits.
main_result: The macroscopic supercurrent inherently contains information about the relative phases of the many-body eigenstates, allowing entanglement to be measured electrically.
method: The supercurrent is analytically derived by decomposing it into static and dynamic (interference) components, utilizing the $\phi$-space Berry connection.
model_or_system: The system involves superconducting nanodevices, specifically Andreev spin qubits coupled via a Josephson junction, modeled using a microscopic wave-function approach beyond Ginzburg-Landau theory.
key_observables: Dynamic Interference Supercurrent ($\delta I$), which oscillates with frequencies related to energy differences between states; the supercurrent itself serves as the diagnostic for entanglement.
important_parameters: Superconducting phase ($\phi$), energy differences between many-body eigenstates ($\omega_1, \omega_2$), and the probability amplitudes ($p_r$) and relative phases ($\vartheta_r$) of the superposition state.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes open boundary conditions and that the population of Andreev bound states does not change with time; it also notes limitations regarding the measurement of maximally entangled Bell states.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time evolution of both the total supercurrent and the DIS for a superposition of multiple eigenstates, and one figure sketches the SQUID setup for detection.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for a microscopic wave-function approach over standard methods, deriving the total supercurrent decomposition ($ ar{I} + \delta I$), and finally demonstrating how the interference term ($\delta I$) allows for the extraction of relative phases necessary for quantum state tomography.
why_interesting: This work directly links a fundamental, macroscopic quantum phenomenon (supercurrent) to the abstract concepts of quantum state tomography and entanglement measurement, providing a concrete, measurable signature for quantum information processing in solid-state devices.
